hook: Training a 7 billion parameter model with Adam needs about 112 gigabytes before a single activation. An H100 has 80.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Training a 7 billion parameter model with Adam needs about 112 gigabytes before a single activation. An H100 has 80.

0:15 QUESTION — Every technique in this module, DDP, ZeRO, FSDP, tensor, pipeline, context and expert parallelism, exists because of one budget. Where do the bytes go? We build the calculator the Ultra-Scale Playbook uses and check it against real tensors.

1:00 INTUITION — Think of GPU memory as a suitcase. The weights are the clothes. Gradients are a second copy of the clothes. Adam packs two more copies plus an fp32 master copy. Activations are the souvenirs you pick up during the forward pass, and they grow with batch and sequence length. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:00 MATH — Mixed-precision Adam per parameter: bf16 weights 2 bytes, bf16 grads 2 bytes, fp32 master weights 4, Adam m 4, Adam v 4. Total 16 bytes, written 2 Psi + 2 Psi + 12 Psi. For Psi = 7e9: 112 GB. ZeRO paper example Psi = 7.5B: 120 GB. Activations per layer without recomputation (Korthikanti et al.): s b h (34 + 5 a s / h) bytes in half precision. Llama-2-7B shape, h = 4096, a = 32, L = 32, s = 4096, b = 1: per layer 4096 * 4096 * (34 + 160) bytes, about 3.25 GB, times 32 layers about 104 GB. Activations dominate at long sequence because of the 5 a s / h attention term, which FlashAttention removes, leaving 34 s b h.

5:00 CODE — def model_memory(psi, mixed=True) -> dict(params, grads, optim). def activation_memory(L, s, b, h, a, flash=False). def total(cfg) reading a HF config.json for Llama 3 8B and Qwen3. Then measure: build your 124M GPT on CPU, run one AdamW step, and sum p.nbytes, p.grad.nbytes and every tensor in optimizer.state.

8:00 RECEIPT — assert measured_bytes == 16 * n_params for fp32 AdamW on the 124M GPT (4 weights + 4 grads + 8 Adam state). assert model_memory(7.5e9)['total'] == 120e9, matching the ZeRO paper's 120 GB baseline. On a CUDA box, the activation formula should land within about 10 percent of torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated minus static memory for a 4-layer model.

10:00 MEASURE — Stacked bar chart: params, grads, optimizer, activations for 1B, 7B, 70B at seq 4096, against an 80 GB line. Second plot: activation memory vs sequence length with and without the attention term.

11:15 TAKEAWAY — Adam training costs 16 bytes per parameter plus activations that scale with batch times sequence. Interview line: a 7B model needs about 112 GB of model state before activations, so you must shard state, shard activations, or both.
12:00 NEXT — Next: Collectives: all-reduce and friends.
key_math: bytes/param = 2 + 2 + 12 = 16 (mixed-precision Adam); M_state = 16 Psi; M_act per layer = s b h (34 + 5 a s / h) bytes; 7e9 * 16 = 112 GB

gotchas: Counting fp32 Adam as 12 bytes and forgetting the gradients; AdamW state is created lazily on the first step, so measuring before step() shows zero optimizer memory; mixing GB (1e9) and GiB (2^30) gives a 7% discrepancy that looks like a bug.
interview_q: How much memory does it take to train a 7B model with Adam in mixed precision? About 16 bytes per parameter for weights, grads, fp32 master weights and two Adam moments, so 112 GB, plus activations that scale with batch times sequence length, which is why a single 80 GB GPU is not enough.
explainer: Here is an eighty gigabyte GPU drawn as a box. Let's fill it with one seven billion parameter model.
The bf16 weights take fourteen gigabytes. That fits easily. Training is where it gets heavy.
Gradients take another fourteen. Then Adam adds an fp32 master copy, momentum and variance, eighty four gigabytes more.
That is sixteen bytes per parameter, one hundred twelve gigabytes in total. We are already over the red line.
Now the forward pass. Every layer saves activations for the backward pass, and they scale with sequence length.
At four thousand tokens, the attention scores alone add a huge block per layer. FlashAttention removes that piece.
Even then, thirty two layers of saved activations need far more room than the GPU has left.
So we have two choices. Split the model state across GPUs, or split the activations. This module does both.

hook: Ring all-reduce sends almost the same bytes per GPU whether you have 8 GPUs or 8000. That is why it runs every training job.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Ring all reduce sends almost the same bytes per GPU whether you have 8 GPUs or 8000. That is why it runs every training job.

0:15 QUESTION — Every parallelism strategy is a choice of which collective to run and when. DDP is all-reduce. FSDP is all-gather plus reduce-scatter. Expert parallelism is all-to-all. Learn the five collectives and their costs and the rest of the module is bookkeeping.

1:00 INTUITION — Eight people in a circle each hold a pie cut into eight slices, and everyone needs the sum of all pies. Pass one slice to your right, add it to yours, repeat. After seven passes each person owns one fully summed slice. That is reduce-scatter. Seven more passes to share the finished slices. That is all-gather. Together, all-reduce. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Collectives on N ranks with message size M: broadcast, reduce, all-reduce, reduce-scatter (each rank ends with 1/N of the sum), all-gather (each rank ends with all N pieces), all-to-all (rank i sends chunk j to rank j). Ring reduce-scatter: N-1 steps, each sends M/N, total (N-1)/N M per rank. All-gather: the same. All-reduce = reduce-scatter + all-gather: 2 (N-1)/N M per rank, which approaches 2M as N grows, independent of N. Alpha-beta time: T = 2(N-1) alpha + 2 (N-1)/N M / beta. Latency term grows with N, which is why large clusters use tree or hierarchical algorithms for small messages. nccl-tests reports busbw = algbw * 2(N-1)/N for all-reduce, so busbw compares to link bandwidth.

5:30 CODE — Single-process simulation first: def ring_reduce_scatter(chunks: list[list[Tensor]]) where chunks[r][c] is rank r's chunk c; at step t rank r sends chunk (r - t) mod N to rank r+1, which adds it. def ring_all_gather(...). def ring_all_reduce = both. Count bytes sent per rank in a counter. def allreduce_time(M, N, alpha, beta).

8:30 RECEIPT — For N in {2, 4, 8} and random tensors: torch.testing.assert_close(ring_all_reduce(xs)[r], sum(xs)) for every rank r. assert bytes_sent_per_rank == 2 * (N-1) / N * M exactly. Then check the busbw convention against the nccl-tests documentation formula, which we use for real numbers in episode 15.

10:30 MEASURE — Plot bytes per rank vs N for naive all-reduce (send everything to rank 0, then broadcast: rank 0 handles (N-1) M twice) vs ring: ring flat near 2M, naive linear in N. Plot alpha-beta time vs message size, showing the latency-bound and bandwidth-bound regimes.

12:00 TAKEAWAY — All-reduce is reduce-scatter plus all-gather, and the ring costs 2(N-1)/N times the message per rank. Interview line: ring all-reduce is bandwidth-optimal because per-rank traffic is nearly independent of world size, but its latency term grows linearly with N.
12:45 NEXT — Next: torch.distributed on your laptop.
key_math: ring RS: (N-1)/N M per rank; ring AG: (N-1)/N M; AR = RS + AG: 2(N-1)/N M; T = 2(N-1) alpha + 2(N-1)/N * M/beta; busbw = algbw * 2(N-1)/N

receipt: torch.testing.assert_close(ring_all_reduce(xs)[r], torch.stack(xs).sum(0)) for all r and N in {2,4,8}; bytes_sent_per_rank == 2*(N-1)/N*M; busbw formula identical to nccl-tests' definition.
gotchas: Off-by-one in the chunk index schedule so a rank adds the same chunk twice; message size not divisible by N, so the last chunk needs padding; confusing algbw (M / time) with busbw when comparing to NVLink specs.
interview_q: Why is ring all-reduce bandwidth-optimal? Each rank sends and receives 2(N-1)/N times the message size, which approaches 2M regardless of N, and no algorithm can do better than about 2M per rank; the cost is 2(N-1) latency steps, so small messages prefer tree algorithms.
explainer: Here are four GPUs in a ring. Each holds its own gradient vector, cut into four chunks.
Step one. Every GPU passes one chunk to its right neighbor, who adds it to its own copy.
Step two and three. Keep passing the running sums around. Each pass moves a quarter of the data.
After three steps, each GPU owns one chunk that holds the sum from everybody. That is reduce scatter.
Now pass the finished chunks around the ring three more times. That is all gather.
Every GPU now has the full sum. Each sent two times three quarters of the vector. That is all reduce.
Grow the ring to sixteen GPUs. The bytes each GPU sends barely change. They approach twice the vector.
What does grow is the number of steps around the ring. For tiny messages, those latency steps dominate the time.

hook: You do not need a GPU cluster to learn distributed training. Four processes on a MacBook run the same collectives NCCL runs.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — You do not need a GPU cluster to learn distributed training. Four processes on a MacBook run the same collectives NCCL runs.

0:15 QUESTION — torch.distributed has a CPU backend called gloo. Same API, same semantics, slower wires. That means every episode from here to episode 14 runs on a laptop, following the way Umar Jamil builds torchfeather. Then we rent four GPUs only when we need real numbers.

1:00 INTUITION — Each process is a pretend GPU with a rank number. A rendezvous address is the meeting point where they find each other. A process group is a phone line between some of them. Collectives are conference calls. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:00 MATH — World size W, rank r in [0, W). torchrun sets RANK, LOCAL_RANK, WORLD_SIZE, MASTER_ADDR, MASTER_PORT. all_reduce of tensor([r]) with SUM gives W(W-1)/2, which is 6 for W = 4. all_gather of [r] gives [0,1,2,3]. reduce_scatter_tensor of arange(W) + r on each rank gives rank r the value 4r + 6. Point-to-point: send and recv, or isend and irecv for non-blocking. Our ring all-reduce from last episode, rebuilt on real processes: N-1 isend/irecv steps for reduce-scatter, N-1 for all-gather.

4:00 CODE — collectives.py: def main(): dist.init_process_group('gloo'); rank = dist.get_rank(); world = dist.get_world_size(). Demo each collective: dist.broadcast, dist.all_reduce, dist.all_gather_into_tensor, dist.reduce_scatter_tensor, dist.all_to_all_single, printing per rank. Launch with torchrun --nproc_per_node=4 collectives.py, and show the mp.spawn alternative with MASTER_ADDR='127.0.0.1'. Then def my_ring_all_reduce(t) using dist.isend to (rank+1) % W and dist.irecv from (rank-1) % W on t.chunk(W). Finally a bandwidth benchmark: all_reduce sizes 1 KB to 64 MB, time.perf_counter around 20 iterations after a dist.barrier().

8:00 RECEIPT — assert all_reduce(tensor([rank])) == W*(W-1)/2 on every rank; assert all_gather result == arange(W); assert reduce_scatter result == 4*rank + 6 for W=4; torch.testing.assert_close(my_ring_all_reduce(x), x_all_reduced_by_dist) for random x of size 1M on all ranks.

10:00 MEASURE — gloo all-reduce algorithm bandwidth vs message size on the Mac: latency-bound below about 64 KB, flat above. Your ring vs dist.all_reduce times side by side; gloo's is faster, explain that it uses tuned algorithms and fewer copies.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — gloo on CPU gives you the real torch.distributed API, so you can build and test every parallelism strategy locally. Interview line: I debug distributed code on CPU with gloo and small world sizes first, then switch the backend to NCCL for performance.
12:15 NEXT — Next: Data parallelism from scratch.
key_math: all_reduce(r) = W(W-1)/2; all_gather -> [0..W-1]; reduce_scatter of (arange(W) + r) gives rank r: sum_k (r + k) over ranks = W r + W(W-1)/2

interview_q: How would you develop and test distributed training code without a GPU cluster? explainer: Here is a MacBook running four Python processes. Each one is a pretend GPU with a rank, zero to three.
They meet at a rendezvous address, localhost and a port, and form one process group.
All reduce. Each rank holds its own rank number. After the call, everyone holds six.

Now we rebuild the ring from last episode with real sends and receives between processes.
Each rank sends to its right neighbor and receives from its left, at the same time, to avoid deadlock.
Our ring and PyTorch's all reduce give identical results. The same code runs on NCCL later.

hook: DDP is about forty lines once you see it: same weights everywhere, different data, average the gradients. The hard part is overlap.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — DDP is about forty lines once you see it. Same weights everywhere, different data, average the gradients. The hard part is overlap.

0:15 QUESTION — Data parallelism is the first strategy every lab uses and the outer loop of every 4D setup. PyTorch's DistributedDataParallel buckets gradients and overlaps the all-reduce with backward. We build ours in steps and prove it trains identically to one process.

1:00 INTUITION — Four students each do a quarter of the homework, then compare answers and average them, so everyone has the same notes for tomorrow. The trick: start comparing the last chapter while still working on the first. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:00 MATH — Global batch B split into W shards of B/W. Loss L = (1/B) sum_i l_i. Rank gradient g_r = (W/B) sum_{i in shard r} grad l_i, the mean over its shard. True gradient = (1/W) sum_r g_r, which is all_reduce(SUM) / W. Communication per step: 2 (W-1)/W * 4 Psi bytes for fp32 grads. Overlap: backward computes gradients last layer first; launch an async all-reduce as soon as a bucket is full, so communication hides behind the rest of backward. Ideal step time max(compute, comm) instead of compute + comm. DDP default bucket size is 25 MB.

4:30 CODE — Version 1, naive: broadcast parameters from rank 0 at init (dist.broadcast(p.data, src=0)); after loss.backward(), for p in params: dist.all_reduce(p.grad); p.grad /= W. Version 2, bucketing: flatten grads into buckets of about 25 MB, one all_reduce per bucket. Version 3, overlap: register p.register_post_accumulate_grad_hook(hook) that adds the param to its bucket and, when full, launches dist.all_reduce(flat, async_op=True) and stores the work handle; before optimizer.step(), wait on all handles and copy back. Use DistributedSampler for the data shards. Train your 124M-style GPT (shrunk to fit CPU) for 20 steps on 4 gloo ranks.

8:30 RECEIPT — Three-way check after 20 steps with the same seed: (a) single process on the full batch, (b) torch.nn.parallel.DistributedDataParallel on 4 ranks, (c) yours on 4 ranks. torch.testing.assert_close on every parameter, (c) vs (a) and (c) vs (b), atol=1e-6 in float32. Also assert parameters are bit-identical across ranks after each step.

10:30 MEASURE — Step time breakdown on gloo for naive, bucketed, overlapped: compute, exposed comm. Number of all-reduce calls per step: one per parameter vs a handful of buckets. On the Mac the overlap gain is modest; we measure the real one on GPUs in episode 15.

12:00 TAKEAWAY — DDP replicates the model, shards the data, and averages gradients with bucketed async all-reduce during backward. Interview line: DDP's speed comes from bucketing to amortize latency and overlapping all-reduce with the backward pass, and its memory cost is a full model copy per GPU.
12:45 NEXT — Next: ZeRO stages 1, 2 and 3.
key_math: g = (1/W) sum_r g_r = all_reduce_sum(g_r)/W; comm bytes/rank = 2(W-1)/W * bytes(grads); T_step ~ max(T_compute, T_comm) with overlap

receipt: After 20 steps torch.testing.assert_close(my_ddp_params, single_process_full_batch_params, atol=1e-6) and against torch.nn.parallel.DistributedDataParallel params; parameters identical across all ranks every step.
gotchas: Forgetting to divide by world size so the effective learning rate is W times larger; unequal shard sizes when the dataset is not divisible by W make ranks disagree about the mean, use drop_last; parameters that receive no gradient in a step never fire their hook, so the bucket never completes and training hangs.
interview_q: How does PyTorch DDP overlap communication with computation? It groups gradients into buckets in reverse parameter order and launches an asynchronous all-reduce for each bucket as soon as all its gradients are computed during backward, so communication for later layers runs while earlier layers are still computing gradients.
explainer: Here are four ranks on our laptop, each process holding an identical copy of the same model.
The batch is split four ways. Each rank runs forward and backward on its own quarter.
Each rank now has a different gradient. Average them with one all reduce, and everyone agrees again.
Same averaged gradient, same optimizer step, so the weights stay exactly identical on every rank.
Doing one all reduce per parameter means hundreds of tiny messages. So we pack gradients into buckets.
Backward runs from the last layer to the first. The last layer's bucket is ready first.
Ship that bucket immediately, while the earlier layers are still computing. Communication now hides behind compute.
After twenty steps, our weights match a single process that trained on the whole batch at once.

hook: ZeRO stage 3 trains a 7.5 billion parameter model on 64 GPUs with under 2 gigabytes of model state each. DDP needs 120.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — ZeRO stage 3 trains a 7.5 billion parameter model on 64 GPUs with under 2 gigabytes of model state each. DDP needs 120.

0:15 QUESTION — DDP keeps a full copy of weights, grads and Adam on every GPU. That is pure redundancy. Microsoft's ZeRO paper removes it in three stages, and FSDP and DeepSpeed are both built on it. We derive the memory formula and implement stage 1.

1:00 INTUITION — Four roommates each own a complete set of kitchen tools. ZeRO says: one roommate owns the pans, one the knives, and you borrow when you need something. Stage 1 shares the optimizer state, stage 2 also the gradients, stage 3 even the weights. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:00 MATH — Per GPU, with Psi params, N_d GPUs, K = 12 for mixed-precision Adam (fp32 master, m, v). DDP: 2 Psi + 2 Psi + K Psi = 16 Psi. ZeRO-1 (P_os): 2 Psi + 2 Psi + K Psi / N_d. ZeRO-2 (P_os+g): 2 Psi + (2 + K) Psi / N_d. ZeRO-3 (P_os+g+p): (2 + 2 + K) Psi / N_d. Paper example Psi = 7.5B, N_d = 64: 120 GB, 31.4 GB, 16.6 GB, 1.9 GB. Communication: DDP all-reduce costs 2 Psi per rank (reduce-scatter + all-gather). ZeRO-1 and 2: reduce-scatter grads, update your shard, all-gather params, also 2 Psi, so free. ZeRO-3: all-gather params in forward, again in backward, reduce-scatter grads: 3 Psi, 1.5x DDP.

5:00 CODE — def zero_memory(psi, n, stage, k=12) returning bytes per GPU, plus a table over n in {1, 8, 64, 1024}. Then ZeRO1Optimizer(params, optim_cls=torch.optim.AdamW, ...) on gloo: flatten all params into one buffer padded to a multiple of W, each rank creates AdamW over only its slice. step(): dist.all_reduce grads (stage 1) or dist.reduce_scatter_tensor into the local slice (stage 2 variant), divide by W, local AdamW step on the shard, dist.all_gather_into_tensor to rebuild full params.

8:30 RECEIPT — assert zero_memory(7.5e9, 64, s) matches the ZeRO paper's 120, 31.4, 16.6, 1.9 GB for s = 0..3 (to one decimal, GB = 1e9). Training: after 20 steps, ZeRO-1 params torch.testing.assert_close to your DDP params from last episode. Production check: wrap the same model with torch.distributed.optim.ZeroRedundancyOptimizer and compare both the parameters and per-rank optimizer state bytes (yours should be about 1/W of AdamW's full state).

10:30 MEASURE — Measured per-rank optimizer state bytes for W in {1, 2, 4}: halves each time. Plot of the formula: per-GPU memory vs N_d for the four configurations, log scale, with an 80 GB line for a 70B model.

12:00 TAKEAWAY — ZeRO removes data-parallel redundancy: stage 1 shards Adam state, stage 2 gradients, stage 3 parameters, for 4 Psi + 12 Psi/N, 2 Psi + 14 Psi/N and 16 Psi/N. Interview line: ZeRO-1 and 2 cost the same communication as DDP, and ZeRO-3 costs 1.5x because parameters are all-gathered in both forward and backward.
12:45 NEXT — Next: FSDP from scratch.
key_math: DDP: (2+2+K) Psi; ZeRO-1: 2Psi + 2Psi + K Psi/N; ZeRO-2: 2Psi + (2+K) Psi/N; ZeRO-3: (2+2+K) Psi/N, K=12; comm: ZeRO-1/2 = 2 Psi, ZeRO-3 = 3 Psi per rank
code_task: zero_memory(psi, n, stage, k=12) and table; ZeRO1Optimizer(params, optim_cls, **kw) with flat padded buffer, per-rank AdamW over its slice, reduce_scatter/all_reduce grads, local step, all_gather_into_tensor params; 4-rank gloo training run.
receipt: zero_memory(7.5e9, 64, stage) == [120, 31.4, 16.6, 1.9] GB matching ZeRO paper Figure 1; torch.testing.assert_close(zero1_params, ddp_params) after 20 steps; parameters and per-rank state bytes compared with torch.distributed.optim.ZeroRedundancyOptimizer.

interview_q: What are ZeRO stages 1, 2 and 3 and what does each cost? explainer: Here is data parallelism on four GPUs. Every GPU holds the same weights, gradients and Adam state.

Stage one cuts the optimizer state into four slices. Each GPU keeps only its own.
After backward, each GPU updates only its slice of the weights, then all gather shares the new weights.
Stage two also slices the gradients. Reduce scatter hands each GPU just the gradient slice it needs.
Stage three slices the weights themselves. A layer's weights are gathered right before use and dropped after.
With sixty four GPUs, memory per GPU falls from one hundred twenty gigabytes to under two.
Stages one and two cost the same communication as plain DDP. Stage three costs about half again more.

hook: FSDP is ZeRO-3 with a schedule: gather a layer's weights just before you need them, throw them away right after.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — FSDP is ZeRO stage 3 with a schedule. Gather a layer's weights just before you need them, throw them away right after.

0:15 QUESTION — Meta trained Llama 3 with FSDP, and PyTorch's torchtitan uses FSDP2's fully_shard as its data-parallel layer. How does it fit a model bigger than any single GPU? We build a mini-FSDP on gloo, then compare to the real fully_shard API.

1:00 INTUITION — Each GPU holds a quarter of every layer, like a book whose pages are split among four friends. To read chapter three, everyone photocopies their pages of chapter three to each other, reads it, then shreds the copies. Only one chapter is ever fully assembled. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:00 MATH — Per FSDP unit (usually one transformer block): forward: all_gather(param shards) -> full params, compute, free full params (reshard_after_forward). Backward: all_gather again, compute grads, reduce_scatter(full grads) -> grad shard, free. Optimizer steps on shards. Peak parameter memory: Psi/N for shards + one or two full units in flight, instead of Psi. Communication per step: AG forward Psi, AG backward Psi, RS Psi, so 3 Psi times bytes, matching ZeRO-3. Prefetching: issue the all-gather for block i+1 while block i computes, to hide latency.

4:30 CODE — class MiniFSDPUnit(nn.Module) wrapping a block: at init, flatten its params into one padded flat tensor, keep only shard = flat.chunk(W)[rank] as an nn.Parameter. forward(x): full = all_gather_into_tensor of shards; set the block's params as views of full (via torch.func.functional_call with a dict of views); out = functional_call(block, params, x); drop full. For backward, wrap in a torch.autograd.Function whose backward re-gathers, recomputes the vjp, and reduce_scatter_tensor's the flat grad into shard.grad divided by W. Then the real thing: from torch.distributed.fsdp import fully_shard; for block in model.blocks: fully_shard(block); fully_shard(model). Show that parameters become DTensors with .to_local() shaped [dim0 / W, ...], and pass mp_policy=MixedPrecisionPolicy(param_dtype=torch.bfloat16, reduce_dtype=torch.float32) on GPU.

8:30 RECEIPT — After 10 steps on 4 gloo ranks: torch.testing.assert_close(mini_fsdp params (gathered), single-process params, atol=1e-6); same comparison for FSDP2 fully_shard on CPU with gloo (it works on CPU device meshes via init_device_mesh('cpu', (4,))). Assert each rank's stored parameter bytes are about total / 4.

10:30 MEASURE — Per-rank parameter plus grad plus optimizer bytes: single process vs DDP vs mini-FSDP vs fully_shard at W = 4. Count of all_gather and reduce_scatter calls per step: 2 x n_blocks and n_blocks.

Interview line: FSDP trades one extra all-gather per step for sharded parameters, and wrapping per transformer block bounds peak memory to the shards plus a block or two of full weights.

explainer: Here is a transformer with four blocks, and four GPUs. Each GPU stores only a quarter of every block.
Forward reaches block one. All four GPUs all gather their quarters, so every GPU briefly has full block one.
Compute block one's output, then throw the gathered weights away. Only each GPU's own quarter remains.
While block one computes, the gather for block two is already in flight. That is prefetching.
Backward runs in reverse order. We gather block four's weights again, then compute its gradients.
Reduce scatter the gradients. Each GPU keeps the summed quarter it owns, and the full copy is dropped.
The optimizer only ever touches quarters. Weights, gradients and Adam state are all sharded four ways.
PyTorch's fully shard does exactly this, one call per block. Our version and theirs match.

hook: Save every fourth layer's input, recompute the rest during backward, and activation memory drops several times for about a third more compute.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Save every block's input, recompute the rest during backward, and activation memory drops several times for about a third more compute.

0:15 QUESTION — FSDP shards model state. Activations still grow with batch and sequence, and at 8k context they dominate. Every large run uses activation checkpointing, full or selective. We measure the exact trade.

1:00 INTUITION — Hiking a trail you plan to walk back on, you can drop a breadcrumb every step, or only at junctions and re-walk short stretches when you return. Fewer breadcrumbs, more walking. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:00 MATH — Without checkpointing: store all intermediate activations, about s b h (34 + 5 a s/h) bytes per layer. Full checkpointing per block: store only each block's input, 2 s b h bytes in bf16, and recompute the block's forward in backward. Compute cost: forward 1x, backward 2x, so training is 3 units; recompute adds 1 forward, giving 4/3, about 33 percent more FLOPs. sqrt(L) checkpointing (Chen et al. 2016): segments of sqrt(L) layers give O(sqrt(L)) memory. Selective checkpointing (Korthikanti et al.): recompute only the cheap but memory-heavy attention softmax and dropout, which removes the 5 a s/h term for a few percent extra compute. With FlashAttention, that part is already recomputed inside the kernel.

4:30 CODE — from torch.utils.checkpoint import checkpoint. In your GPT forward: x = checkpoint(block, x, use_reentrant=False) when cfg.ckpt == 'full'; every k-th block for 'every_k'. Also a manual version: class Recompute(torch.autograd.Function) that saves only the input in forward under torch.no_grad() and reruns block forward with grad enabled in backward. Measurement script: on GPU torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated; on Mac count bytes saved for backward with torch.autograd.graph.saved_tensors_hooks(pack, unpack) summing t.nbytes.

8:00 RECEIPT — Gradients identical: torch.testing.assert_close(grads with checkpoint, grads without, atol=0, rtol=0) in float32 with dropout off (bitwise for deterministic CPU ops). Saved-tensor bytes per block without checkpointing within 10 percent of the s b h (34 + 5 a s / h) formula adapted to fp32 and your block's exact ops, and with full checkpointing equal to the block input bytes.
10:00 MEASURE — Table for a 12-layer GPT: none, every-2, full: saved bytes, step time, tokens/s. Expect full checkpointing near 4/3 step time. Plot max batch size that fits vs strategy.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — Checkpointing stores block inputs and recomputes the forward in backward, about 33 percent more compute for most of the activation memory back. Interview line: full checkpointing costs one extra forward, selective checkpointing targets memory-heavy, compute-light ops like attention softmax for a much smaller overhead.

interview_q: What does activation checkpointing cost and when is selective checkpointing better? Full checkpointing stores only block inputs and reruns each block's forward in backward, roughly 33% more compute; selective checkpointing recomputes only memory-heavy, cheap ops like the attention softmax, recovering most of the memory for a few percent extra compute.
explainer: Here is a forward pass through twelve blocks. Each block leaves a pile of saved activations for backward.
Stack those piles up. At long sequence lengths, they are bigger than the whole model itself.
Checkpointing keeps only each block's input, one thin slice per block. Everything else is discarded.
Backward reaches block twelve. We rerun its forward from the saved input, rebuilding the pile just for this block.
Use those activations to get gradients, then discard them again and move to block eleven.
The price is one extra forward pass. Training goes from three units of compute to four.
Selective checkpointing is pickier. It only recomputes the attention softmax, which is huge in memory but cheap in math.
The gradients come out bit for bit identical to before. We simply traded extra compute for memory.

hook: Split a matrix by columns and the GPUs never need to talk. Split the next one by rows and one all-reduce finishes the job.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Split a matrix by columns and the GPUs never need to talk. Split the next one by rows and one all reduce finishes the job.

0:15 QUESTION — When a single layer's weights or activations are too big for one GPU, you split the matrix itself. Megatron-LM's column and row parallel linear layers are the building block of every tensor-parallel model, including how vLLM serves big models. We build both and check them against an unsharded layer.

1:00 INTUITION — Multiplying by a matrix is a bunch of independent dot products. Give each GPU some of the output columns, and each computes its slice of the output alone. Or give each GPU some input rows, and each computes a partial sum of the full output, which then needs adding up. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:00 MATH — Y = X A, X is (b, d_in), A is (d_in, d_out). Column parallel: A = [A_1, ..., A_N] split along d_out. Y_i = X A_i, Y = [Y_1, ..., Y_N]. Forward needs X replicated, no communication; output is sharded. Backward: dX = sum_i dY_i A_i^T, so an all-reduce on dX. Row parallel: A split along d_in into A_i stacked, X split along its last dim into X_i. Y = sum_i X_i A_i, so an all-reduce in forward; backward dX_i = dY A_i^T is local. Megatron's conjugate operators: f is identity in forward and all-reduce in backward; g is all-reduce in forward and identity in backward. Column followed by row: the sharded output of the first feeds the second directly, so a whole MLP needs one all-reduce forward and one backward.

4:30 CODE — class _CopyToTP(torch.autograd.Function): forward returns x, backward all_reduces grad (that is f). class _ReduceFromTP: forward all_reduces, backward identity (that is g). class ColumnParallelLinear(d_in, d_out, gather_output=False): weight shard (d_out/W, d_in) from the full init via chunk(W, dim=0)[rank]; forward: F.linear(_CopyToTP.apply(x), w_shard). class RowParallelLinear(d_in, d_out): weight shard (d_out, d_in/W) via chunk(W, dim=1)[rank]; forward: _ReduceFromTP.apply(F.linear(x_shard, w_shard)) plus bias once after the reduce. Initialize the full weight with the same seed on every rank, then slice, so you can compare.

8:00 RECEIPT — On 4 gloo ranks: torch.testing.assert_close(row(col(x)), unsharded_linear2(unsharded_linear1(x)), atol=1e-6), and gradients: gathered weight grads and dX match the unsharded backward. Production cross-check: apply torch.distributed.tensor.parallel.parallelize_module(model, mesh, {'fc1': ColwiseParallel(), 'fc2': RowwiseParallel()}) on a CPU DeviceMesh and assert_close its outputs with yours.

10:00 MEASURE — Communication count per forward and backward for the two-layer MLP: col+row 1 + 1 all-reduce vs row+col (wrong order) requiring an extra all-gather. Bytes per all-reduce: b * s * d_model elements.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — Column parallel splits outputs with no forward communication, row parallel splits inputs and needs an all-reduce, and chaining them costs one all-reduce each way. Interview line: Megatron pairs a column-parallel then a row-parallel linear so the intermediate activation stays sharded and the only sync is a single all-reduce.
12:15 NEXT — Next: Tensor-parallel attention and MLP.
key_math: Column: A = [A_1..A_N], Y_i = X A_i (no comm fwd, AR on dX bwd); Row: Y = sum_i X_i A_i (AR fwd, local bwd); f: id fwd / AR bwd, g: AR fwd / id bwd

receipt: torch.testing.assert_close(row(col(x)), lin2(lin1(x)), atol=1e-6) plus input and gathered weight gradients on 4 gloo ranks; outputs equal to torch.distributed.tensor.parallel ColwiseParallel/RowwiseParallel on a CPU DeviceMesh.
gotchas: Adding the row-parallel bias on every rank before the all-reduce so it is counted W times; nn.Linear stores weight as (out, in), so column parallel chunks dim 0 and row parallel chunks dim 1, the reverse of the math notation; forgetting the backward all-reduce in f, giving correct outputs but wrong input gradients.
interview_q: How does Megatron tensor parallelism split an MLP and how many collectives does it need? The first linear is column-parallel so each GPU computes a slice of the hidden layer and applies GeLU locally; the second is row-parallel, producing partial sums combined by one all-reduce; total one all-reduce in forward and one in backward.
explainer: Here is a matrix multiply. X times A gives Y. We want to split it across two GPUs.
Cut A down the middle by columns. Each GPU gets half the columns and the full X.
Each GPU computes half of Y by itself. No talking needed. The output is split by columns.
Now cut a matrix by rows instead. Each GPU gets half the rows and the matching half of the input.
Each GPU computes a full sized Y, but it is only a partial sum. One all reduce adds them up.
Chain them. The column split output is exactly the row split input. It flows straight through.
A whole MLP costs one all reduce forward. Backward mirrors it, with one all reduce at the start.
Our sharded MLP and the full unsharded one give the same outputs and the same gradients.

hook: A tensor-parallel transformer block needs exactly two all-reduces in its forward pass: one after attention, one after the MLP.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — A tensor parallel transformer block needs exactly two all reduces in its forward pass. One after attention, one after the MLP.

0:15 QUESTION — Last episode we split one MLP. Attention splits even more naturally, because heads are already independent. Megatron's full block layout is how 70B-class models train within a node. We build a TP block for your GPT and run it on 4 gloo ranks.

1:00 INTUITION — Multi-head attention is already a team of independent heads. Give each GPU a group of heads. Each GPU does its heads start to finish, and only at the output projection do they add up their contributions. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:00 MATH — Attention: W_Q, W_K, W_V column-parallel by heads: GPU i holds heads in group i, H/N heads. Each computes softmax(Q_i K_i^T / sqrt(d)) V_i locally. W_O is row-parallel over the concatenated head dim, so output = sum_i O_i W_O,i, one all-reduce. MLP with SwiGLU: W_gate and W_up column-parallel, silu(gate) * up elementwise on the local shard, W_down row-parallel, one all-reduce. Per block forward: 2 all-reduces of b s h elements, backward: 2 more. GQA constraint: N must divide n_kv_heads. Sequence parallelism (Korthikanti): in LayerNorm and dropout regions shard along sequence, turning each all-reduce into reduce-scatter plus all-gather, same bytes, activation memory in those regions divided by N.

4:30 CODE — class TPAttention: wq, wk, wv = ColumnParallelLinear(d, n_heads*hd) etc., local n_heads // W heads, F.scaled_dot_product_attention(is_causal=True) on local heads, wo = RowParallelLinear(n_heads*hd, d). class TPSwiGLU with gate, up column-parallel and down row-parallel. class TPBlock with RMSNorms replicated. load_from_full(block, full_block, rank, W) that slices a single-GPU block's weights so we can compare. Run 4 ranks: 4 heads per rank for a 16-head block.

8:00 RECEIPT — torch.testing.assert_close(tp_block(x), full_block(x), atol=1e-5) in float32 on each rank, plus loss.backward() with gathered grads equal to the full block's grads. Count collectives with a wrapper around dist.all_reduce: exactly 2 in forward, 2 in backward per block. Cross-check with parallelize_module using ColwiseParallel for wq, wk, wv, w_gate, w_up and RowwiseParallel for wo, w_down.

10:00 MEASURE — Per-rank parameter bytes (about 1/4 for the attention and MLP weights, norms replicated). Activation memory per rank in attention: 1/4 because heads are split. All-reduce bytes per block per step vs model dimension.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — Shard attention by heads and the MLP by hidden units, column then row, for two all-reduces per block each way. Interview line: tensor parallelism needs high-bandwidth links because it all-reduces activations twice per block per pass, so it is used within a node, not across nodes.
12:15 NEXT — Next: Pipeline parallelism and the bubble.
key_math: Attention: heads split, O = sum_i O_i W_O,i (1 AR); MLP: gate/up column, down row (1 AR); per block 2 AR fwd + 2 AR bwd of b*s*h elements; N | n_kv_heads

interview_q: Why is tensor parallelism usually limited to within a node? Each transformer block all-reduces the full activation tensor twice in forward and twice in backward, so communication volume scales with batch times sequence times hidden, which needs NVLink-class bandwidth; across slower inter-node links it stalls compute.
explainer: Here is one transformer block, attention then MLP, with sixteen heads, and four GPUs to split it across.
Give each GPU four heads. Its slices of the query, key and value weights produce only those heads.
Each GPU runs attention on its four heads completely on its own. Heads never need each other.
The output projection is split by rows. Each GPU produces a partial output, and one all reduce sums them.
The MLP follows the same pattern. Gate and up are split by columns, down by rows. One more all reduce.
That is two all reduces forward per block, and two in backward. Every one moves the full activation tensor.
That is why tensor parallelism lives inside a node, on NVLink, and not across slow network links.
Our four way block matches the single GPU block exactly, in both its outputs and its gradients.

hook: Split a model across 4 GPUs by layers and, done naively, each GPU sits idle three quarters of the time. Micro-batches shrink that bubble.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Split a model across 4 GPUs by layers and, done naively, each GPU sits idle three quarters of the time. Micro batches shrink that bubble.

0:15 QUESTION — Tensor parallelism needs fast links. Pipeline parallelism needs only point-to-point sends between neighbors, so it works across nodes. GPipe made it practical. We derive the bubble fraction, build a schedule simulator, and run a real 4-stage pipeline on gloo.

1:00 INTUITION — An assembly line with four stations. If one car goes through at a time, three stations always wait. Send many small cars in a row and all stations stay busy, except while the line fills up at the start and drains at the end. That fill and drain is the bubble. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:00 MATH — p stages, m micro-batches, t_f and t_b forward and backward time per micro-batch per stage. GPipe: all forwards, then all backwards. Total time (m + p - 1)(t_f + t_b). Useful time m (t_f + t_b). Bubble fraction of total: (p - 1) / (m + p - 1). The Ultra-Scale Playbook writes the overhead relative to ideal as (p - 1)/m. p = 4, m = 1: 75 percent idle. p = 4, m = 16: 3/19, about 16 percent. Memory: GPipe holds activations for all m micro-batches at once before backward starts. Communication: send activations of size b_micro * s * h forward, gradients of that size backward, between neighbors only.

4:30 CODE — Simulator: def simulate(schedule: list[list[op]], p, m, tf=1, tb=2) where op = ('F' or 'B', microbatch), respecting dependencies: F(i, s) after F(i, s-1), B(i, s) after B(i, s+1) and F(i, s). Returns per-stage timelines; draw them as a Gantt chart with matplotlib. def gpipe_schedule(p, m). Real pipeline on 4 gloo ranks: split your GPT's blocks into 4 stages; each rank loops forwards with dist.recv of activations from rank-1 and dist.send to rank+1, keeping outputs; then backwards in reverse using torch.autograd.backward(out, grad_from_next) and sending input.grad to rank-1. Accumulate grads over m micro-batches.

8:30 RECEIPT — Simulator: assert measured idle fraction == (p-1)/(m+p-1) for p in {2,4,8}, m in {1,4,16,64} when tb = tf, and still exactly that with tb = 2 tf. Real pipeline: after one step, gathered gradients torch.testing.assert_close to single-process gradients on the same full batch (atol=1e-6). Optional production check: torch.distributed.pipelining's ScheduleGPipe gives the same gradients.
10:30 MEASURE — Gantt charts for m = 1, 4, 16 with bubble shaded. Plot bubble fraction vs m for p = 4 and 8 against the formula. Peak stored activations per stage vs m: linear in m for GPipe.

12:00 TAKEAWAY — Pipeline parallelism splits layers across GPUs, and the idle fraction is (p-1)/(m+p-1), so you want many micro-batches. Interview line: GPipe reduces the bubble with micro-batching, but stores activations for every micro-batch, which is the problem 1F1B fixes.
12:45 NEXT — Next: 1F1B and zero-bubble schedules.
key_math: T_GPipe = (m + p - 1)(t_f + t_b); bubble = (p - 1)/(m + p - 1); overhead vs ideal = (p - 1)/m; activations held per stage: m micro-batches

gotchas: Receiving into a tensor of the wrong shape or dtype hangs or corrupts silently, send shapes once up front; detaching the received activation without requires_grad_() so no gradient flows back to the previous stage; averaging the loss per micro-batch instead of over the full batch makes gradients m times too large.
interview_q: What is the pipeline bubble and how do you reduce it? With p stages, the first and last p-1 slots of a step leave stages idle while the pipe fills and drains, giving a bubble of (p-1)/(m+p-1) of the step time with m micro-batches; you reduce it with more micro-batches, interleaved stages, or zero-bubble schedules.
explainer: Here is our model cut into four stages, one per GPU, like stations on an assembly line.
Send one batch through. GPU one works, then two, then three, then four. Then backward, in reverse.
Draw it as a timeline. Most of the chart is empty. Each GPU is idle three quarters of the time.
Now cut the batch into small micro batches, and stream them into the pipeline one after another.
The pipeline fills, runs full, then drains. Empty triangles remain at the start and end. That is the bubble.
With p stages and m micro batches, the bubble is p minus one over m plus p minus one.
Four stages and sixteen micro batches leaves about sixteen percent idle. More micro batches, smaller bubble.
The catch is memory. Every stage holds activations for all sixteen micro batches before backward even begins.

hook: 1F1B has the exact same bubble as GPipe. Its win is memory: each stage holds at most p micro-batches, not all m.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — 1F1B has the exact same bubble as GPipe. Its win is memory. Each stage holds at most p micro batches, not all m.

0:15 QUESTION — Megatron-LM, DeepSpeed and torchtitan all default to 1F1B-family schedules, and DeepSeek-V3 used its own DualPipe. Why reorder the same forwards and backwards? We draw the schedules, prove the bubble math, and measure activation memory.

1:00 INTUITION — GPipe is like doing all the dishes' washing, then all the drying. Your counter fills with wet dishes. 1F1B washes one, dries one, so the counter never holds more than a few. Same total work, same start-up delay, far less counter space. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:00 MATH — 1F1B: stage s does p - s warm-up forwards (s from 1), then alternates one forward, one backward, then cools down with the remaining backwards. Bubble is still (p-1)/(m+p-1) of time. In-flight micro-batches on stage 1: at most p, versus m for GPipe. So activation memory goes from m * A to p * A. Interleaved 1F1B (Megatron, v virtual stages per GPU, each GPU owns v non-contiguous chunks of layers): bubble overhead drops to (p-1)/(v m), at the cost of v times more point-to-point communication. Zero-bubble (Qi et al. 2023): split backward into B (gradient w.r.t. input, on the critical path) and W (gradient w.r.t. weights, can be deferred), and fill bubbles with W work, approaching zero bubble. DualPipe in DeepSeek-V3 runs micro-batches from both ends and overlaps compute with communication.

5:00 CODE — Extend the simulator: def one_f_one_b_schedule(p, m), def interleaved_schedule(p, m, v), def zb_h1_schedule(p, m) with ops F, B, W (W time = B time = tf as a simple model). Track per-stage peak in-flight micro-batches. Then convert your gloo pipeline from last episode to 1F1B order: warm-up loop, steady-state loop with isend/irecv pairs, cool-down loop.

8:30 RECEIPT — Simulator: assert bubble(1F1B) == (p-1)/(m+p-1) == bubble(GPipe); assert peak in-flight on stage 1 == min(p, m) for 1F1B and == m for GPipe; interleaved bubble overhead == (p-1)/(v m) within simulator granularity. Real pipeline: 1F1B gradients torch.testing.assert_close to GPipe and single-process gradients, and measured peak saved-activation bytes (saved_tensors_hooks counter) on stage 1 drop from about m units to p units. Optional: torch.distributed.pipelining Schedule1F1B gradients equal.

10:30 MEASURE — Four Gantt charts at p = 4, m = 8: GPipe, 1F1B, interleaved v = 2, zero-bubble H1. Table: bubble fraction and peak activations per stage. Plot measured activation bytes on stage 1 vs m for GPipe and 1F1B.

12:00 TAKEAWAY — 1F1B keeps GPipe's bubble but caps in-flight activations at p; interleaving shrinks the bubble by v, and zero-bubble fills it with deferred weight-gradient work. Interview line: splitting backward into input-grad and weight-grad lets the weight-grad part fill pipeline bubbles.
12:45 NEXT — Next: Context parallelism and ring attention.
key_math: 1F1B bubble = (p-1)/(m+p-1) (same as GPipe); peak in-flight = p (vs m); interleaved overhead = (p-1)/(v m); zero-bubble: backward = B (input grad) + W (weight grad), W deferred

receipt: bubble(1F1B) == bubble(GPipe) == (p-1)/(m+p-1); peak in-flight stage 1: 1F1B == min(p, m), GPipe == m; 1F1B pipeline grads torch.testing.assert_close single-process grads; measured stage-1 saved-activation bytes scale with p not m.
gotchas: Deadlock in steady state when neighbor stages both block on send, pair isend/irecv or use batch_isend_irecv; warm-up count off by one per stage, stage s needs p - s - 1 warm-up forwards with zero-indexed s; freeing a micro-batch's activations before its backward ran.
interview_q: If 1F1B has the same bubble as GPipe, why use it? Because it starts backward passes as soon as possible, each stage holds activations for at most p micro-batches instead of all m, so you can use many micro-batches to shrink the bubble without running out of memory.
explainer: Here is the GPipe schedule on four stages and eight micro batches. All forwards first, then all backwards.
Watch stage one's memory. It climbs with every forward and holds all eight micro batches at the peak.
Now 1F1B. Stage one does a few warm up forwards, then alternates. One forward, one backward.
As soon as a backward finishes, that micro batch's activations are freed. Memory plateaus at four.
Look at the idle triangles. They are exactly the same size as GPipe's. The bubble did not change.
Interleaved 1F1B gives each GPU two smaller chunks of layers. The bubble shrinks by half.
Zero bubble splits backward in two. Input gradients go first. Weight gradients wait and fill the gaps.
Same math and same gradients, just a different order. The order alone decides memory and idle time.

hook: Ring attention trains on sequences no single GPU could hold. Each GPU keeps its slice of queries and passes keys and values around a ring.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Ring attention trains on sequences no single GPU could hold. Each GPU keeps its slice of queries and passes keys and values around a ring.

0:15 QUESTION — Million-token context models need the sequence itself split across GPUs. Llama 3 used context parallelism for long-context training. The math is the online softmax we derived for FlashAttention, now across GPUs instead of across tiles. We build it on gloo and match full attention exactly.

1:00 INTUITION — Each GPU is a FlashAttention program that owns a block of queries. Instead of streaming K and V tiles from HBM, it receives them from its neighbor, attends, folds the result in with online softmax, and passes them on. After N hops every query has seen every key. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:00 MATH — Split sequence into N chunks; rank r holds Q_r, K_r, V_r. Step t = 0..N-1: rank r holds KV chunk j = (r - t) mod N. Compute block attention o_t, lse_t for Q_r against K_j, V_j. Merge: lse_new = log(exp(lse) + exp(lse_t)), o = exp(lse - lse_new) o + exp(lse_t - lse_new) o_t. Send current KV to rank r+1, receive from r-1, overlapped with compute. Per step compute ~ 4 (S/N)^2 d, comm 2 (S/N) d per rank: compute grows quadratically in chunk length and comm linearly, so for long enough chunks comm hides fully. Causal: chunk j > r is fully masked, so naive splitting idles rank 0 and overloads rank N-1. Zigzag fix: split into 2N chunks and give rank r chunks r and 2N-1-r so every rank has equal causal work.

5:00 CODE — def block_attn(q, k, v, causal_mode) -> (o, lse) using your flash_fwd_ref from M08 or SDPA plus a manual logsumexp. def merge(o, lse, o_t, lse_t). def ring_attention(q_local, k_local, v_local, causal): loop N steps with dist.isend(kv_buf, (rank+1)%N) and dist.irecv(next_buf, (rank-1)%N) launched before compute, wait after. Causal handling per step: j == r diagonal mask, j < r full, j > r skip. Zigzag reorder helpers shard_zigzag(x) and unshard_zigzag(x).

8:30 RECEIPT — On 4 gloo ranks with S = 1024, d = 64: gather outputs and torch.testing.assert_close(ring_out, F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q,k,v,is_causal=causal), atol=1e-5) for causal in {False, True}, both contiguous and zigzag sharding. Backward via autograd through the loop (or a manual ring backward that also passes dK, dV around) matches SDPA gradients. Work balance: count unmasked score elements per rank; zigzag makes them equal.

10:30 MEASURE — Per-rank unmasked FLOPs, contiguous vs zigzag, bar chart. Per-rank memory for the attention part: O(S/N) instead of O(S). Compute-vs-comm time per step on gloo as chunk size grows, showing where communication becomes hidden.

12:00 TAKEAWAY — Ring attention shards the sequence, rotates KV around a ring, and merges partial results with logsumexp, exactly like FlashAttention tiles. Interview line: context parallelism needs load balancing for causal masks, which zigzag sharding solves by pairing an early chunk with a late chunk on each rank.
12:45 NEXT — Next: Expert parallelism and all-to-all.
key_math: KV chunk at step t: j = (r - t) mod N; lse_new = log(e^{lse} + e^{lse_t}); o = e^{lse - lse_new} o + e^{lse_t - lse_new} o_t; compute/step ~ 4 (S/N)^2 d vs comm ~ 2 (S/N) d; zigzag: rank r gets chunks r and 2N-1-r
code_task: block_attn(q,k,v,mode) -> (o, lse); merge(o, lse, o_t, lse_t); ring_attention(q_local, k_local, v_local, causal) with isend/irecv overlapped with compute; shard_zigzag / unshard_zigzag; gloo test harness gathering outputs.
receipt: torch.testing.assert_close(gathered ring_attention output, F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q,k,v,is_causal=causal), atol=1e-5) for causal and non-causal, contiguous and zigzag; gradients match SDPA; equal unmasked work per rank under zigzag.
gotchas: Overwriting the KV buffer you are still computing on with the incoming one, double-buffer it; causal masking with local indices instead of global positions after zigzag reordering; merging with lse = -inf from a fully skipped block produces nan, initialize carefully and skip merges.
interview_q: How does ring attention compute exact attention over a sequence split across GPUs? Each GPU keeps its query chunk and passes key-value chunks around a ring; at each step it computes block attention and merges it into a running output using logsumexp-weighted online softmax, overlapping the KV transfer with compute, so after N steps it has exact attention.
explainer: Here is a sequence of one thousand tokens, too long for one GPU. We cut it into four chunks, one per GPU.
Each GPU holds its own queries, keys and values. Queries stay put for the whole computation.
Step one. Each GPU attends its queries to its own keys and values, and keeps a partial output and log sum exp.
Then every GPU passes its keys and values to the right, and receives a new chunk from the left.
Attend to the new chunk and merge with the online softmax rule from module eight. Same formula.
After four steps, every query has seen every key. The output is exact, not approximate.
With a causal mask, the last GPU does all the work and the first sits idle. That is unbalanced.
Zigzag sharding gives each GPU one early chunk and one late chunk. Every GPU does equal work.

hook: In expert parallelism every token takes a round trip across GPUs: out to its experts, then back home, with two all-to-alls per MoE layer.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — In expert parallelism every token takes a round trip across GPUs. Out to its experts, then back home. Two all to alls per MoE layer.

0:15 QUESTION — DeepSeek-V3 has 256 routed experts per layer; no GPU holds them all. Expert parallelism puts different experts on different GPUs and ships tokens to them. DeepSeek even wrote a custom library, DeepEP, just for this communication. We build dispatch and combine with all_to_all_single on gloo.

1:00 INTUITION — A post office. Each GPU sorts its outgoing tokens into mailbags by destination GPU, everyone swaps bags in one exchange, experts process their mail, then a second exchange sends everything back to the original sender in the original order. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:00 MATH — E experts over N ranks, E/N per rank. Each rank routes its T local tokens with top-k, producing T k assignments. send_counts[j] = number of assignments to experts on rank j. First all-to-all exchanges counts (so receivers can allocate), second exchanges the token vectors: rank r sends send_counts[j] rows to rank j. Experts run on received tokens. Combine: reverse all-to-all with the swapped split sizes, then weight by gates and sum the k contributions per token. Bytes per rank per layer about 2 * T k h * bytes (dispatch plus combine), forward only; backward doubles it. Load imbalance means some ranks receive far more tokens, which is why balancing from M09E07 matters, and why DeepSeek-V3 limits each token to experts on at most 4 nodes.

4:30 CODE — def dispatch(x (T,h), topk_idx (T,k), experts_per_rank): flatten assignments, sort by destination rank with argsort, compute send_counts via torch.bincount; dist.all_to_all_single(recv_counts, send_counts); then dist.all_to_all_single(recv_x, x_sorted, output_split_sizes=recv_counts.tolist(), input_split_sizes=send_counts.tolist()). Also send local expert ids so the receiver knows which of its experts to apply. def local_experts(recv_x, recv_eid). def combine(y, ...): reverse all_to_all_single with swapped splits, unsort with the inverse permutation, out.index_add_ weighted by gates. EPMoE module that wraps all of it, with each rank holding E/N experts.

8:30 RECEIPT — On 4 gloo ranks with E = 8 experts, top-2: build the same MoE single-process (your M09E06 layer, same seeds), and torch.testing.assert_close(ep_moe(x_local), single_moe(x_full)[rank slice], atol=1e-5), plus gradients on expert weights equal after an all-gather. Assert sum of recv_counts over ranks == T_total * k.

10:30 MEASURE — Tokens received per rank per step under three routers from M09E07 (plain, aux, bias): max/mean ratio. Bytes moved per all-to-all vs T k h. Time split on gloo: routing, dispatch, expert compute, combine.

12:00 TAKEAWAY — Expert parallelism places experts on different ranks and uses one all-to-all to dispatch tokens and another to combine them. Interview line: EP communication is all-to-all and its cost scales with tokens times top-k times hidden size, so load imbalance directly becomes stragglers.
12:45 NEXT — Next: Device meshes: combining 3D/4D parallelism.
key_math: send_counts[j] = #assignments to experts on rank j; sum_j recv_counts = received assignments; bytes/rank/layer ~ 2 T k h b (dispatch + combine, forward); experts per rank = E/N

receipt: torch.testing.assert_close(ep_moe(x_local), single_process_moe(x_full)[rank_slice], atol=1e-5) and matching expert weight gradients; sum of recv_counts across ranks == T_total * k.
gotchas: Passing split sizes as tensors instead of Python lists to all_to_all_single; forgetting the inverse permutation so outputs come back in destination order rather than original token order; a rank receiving zero tokens must still participate in every all-to-all or the group hangs.
interview_q: How does expert parallelism move tokens to experts on other GPUs? After routing, each rank sorts token copies by the rank that hosts their chosen experts, exchanges counts and then token vectors with an all-to-all, runs its local experts, and sends results back with a reverse all-to-all, where they are gate-weighted and summed.
explainer: Here are four GPUs, each holding two of eight experts, and each holding its own batch of tokens.
The router picks two experts for every token. Many of those experts live on other GPUs.
Each GPU sorts its outgoing token copies into four mailbags, one for every destination GPU.
First, everyone exchanges just the bag sizes, so each GPU knows how much mail is coming.
Then one all to all swaps the bags. Every GPU now holds the tokens its experts need.
The experts process their received tokens locally. This is the only real compute in the whole layer.
A second all to all sends results home. Each GPU unsorts them and adds the two expert outputs per token.
If one expert is too popular, its GPU gets a giant bag and everyone waits. Balance is a speed issue.

hook: Eight GPUs, three kinds of parallelism, and every collective must go to the right subset. A device mesh is the map that keeps it straight.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Eight GPUs, three kinds of parallelism, and every collective must go to the right subset. A device mesh is the map that keeps it straight.

0:15 QUESTION — Llama 3 405B trained on 16 thousand GPUs with 4D parallelism: tensor, pipeline, context and data. torchtitan expresses all of it with DeviceMesh. Which ranks talk to which, and why does tensor parallel go on the fastest links? We lay out 8 ranks on the Mac and prove every group is right. This is the core of P3, feathertrain.

1:00 INTUITION — Arrange GPUs in a 3D grid. Each axis is one kind of parallelism. Moving along the TP axis you meet your tensor-parallel partners, along DP your data-parallel replicas. Each axis gets its own process groups. Put the chattiest axis, TP, inside a node where links are fastest. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:00 MATH — World size W = dp * pp * tp (* cp). Rank layout with tp innermost: rank = ((d * pp) + p) * tp + t. TP group for fixed (d, p): {(d*pp + p)*tp + t for t in range(tp)}, contiguous ranks, same node. Communication volume per step, rough: TP 4 all-reduces of b s h per block (high, every layer), CP KV passes per attention layer, PP point-to-point b s h per micro-batch at stage boundaries (low), DP one gradient all-reduce or reduce-scatter of Psi/(tp pp) per step (large but once, overlappable). Hence order: TP innermost (NVLink), then CP, PP, and DP outermost across nodes. Memory: params per GPU about Psi / (tp * pp), divided further by dp under FSDP.

4:30 CODE — Launch 8 processes with torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 on gloo. mesh = init_device_mesh('cpu', (2, 2, 2), mesh_dim_names=('dp', 'pp', 'tp')). Print, for each rank, mesh['tp'].get_group() ranks via dist.get_process_group_ranks, and the same for 'pp' and 'dp'. Write my_groups(dp, pp, tp) computing the groups by hand with the formula and create them with dist.new_group. Then a tiny 3D run: your TP block from E09 on the 'tp' group, 2 pipeline stages over 'pp', gradient all-reduce over 'dp'. Pass group=... to every collective.

8:30 RECEIPT — assert my_groups(2,2,2) == the groups DeviceMesh produced, for every rank and every dim. Collective test: all_reduce(tensor([rank]), group=tp_group) equals the sum over that rank's TP group, and similarly for pp and dp. End-to-end: the 3D-parallel tiny GPT's loss after 5 steps torch.testing.assert_close to single-process training on the same global batch.

interview_q: How do you lay out 3D parallelism across a cluster? explainer: Here are eight GPUs in a row. On their own they are just ranks zero through seven.
Fold them into a two by two by two cube. Each axis is one kind of parallelism.
Along the short axis, pairs of neighbors form tensor parallel groups. They talk every single layer.
Along the next axis sit the pipeline groups. They pass activations only at stage boundaries.
Along the last axis sit the data parallel replicas. They sync gradients just once per step.
So we put the chattiest axis, tensor parallel, on the fastest wires, inside a single node.
Every collective now names its group. A tensor parallel all reduce never touches the data parallel partners.
Our hand built groups match DeviceMesh exactly, and the three D run matches single GPU training.

hook: On four real GPUs, DDP scales almost perfectly for a small model, and tensor parallelism over PCIe can make the same model slower.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — On four real GPUs, DDP scales almost perfectly for a small model, and tensor parallelism over PCIe can make the same model slower.

0:15 QUESTION — Everything so far ran on gloo, where correctness transfers and speed does not. Now we rent four GPUs on RunPod, switch to NCCL, and measure tokens per second and scaling efficiency for DDP, FSDP and TP with the same model. Real numbers for the feathertrain report.

1:00 INTUITION — Scaling efficiency asks: with four times the GPUs, do you get four times the tokens per second? Communication is the tax. Whether the tax is small depends on the links between GPUs, NVLink or PCIe, and on how much compute you have to hide it behind. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:00 MATH — Scaling efficiency eta(N) = throughput(N) / (N * throughput(1)), measured at fixed per-GPU batch (weak scaling). DDP comm per step 2 (N-1)/N * 2 Psi bytes in bf16; at Psi = 350M that is about 1 GB per step per GPU; hidden if step compute is longer than comm time at the measured bus bandwidth. TP comm per step 4 L b s h * 2 bytes per GPU per micro-step, every layer, hard to hide. Bus bandwidth from nccl-tests: busbw = algbw * 2(N-1)/N for all-reduce. Expected link speeds: PCIe 4.0 x16 about 32 GB/s per direction (lower peer-to-peer in practice), NVLink on A100 SXM about 600 GB/s total.

4:30 CODE — RunPod: 4x GPU pod; first record nvidia-smi topo -m to see whether links are NVLink or PCIe. Run nccl-tests all_reduce_perf -b 8M -e 1G -f 2 -g 1 under mpirun or one process per GPU and record busbw. Then train.py --strategy {single, ddp, fsdp, tp, fsdp+tp} on a ~350M GPT, bf16, torch.compile, fixed micro-batch per GPU, backend='nccl'. Use torch.nn.parallel.DistributedDataParallel, fully_shard, and parallelize_module for the production versions, and your own implementations from E04, E06, E09 for comparison. Log tokens/s averaged over steps 20 to 100, torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated, and a torch.profiler trace for one step per strategy.

8:30 RECEIPT — Measured nccl-tests busbw within the expected range for the detected topology (record it, it is the ceiling for everything else). Loss curves of ddp, fsdp, tp over 200 steps overlap the single-GPU curve on the same global batch (within bf16 noise). Your DDP and FSDP tokens/s within some percent of PyTorch's; report the gap honestly and explain it from the profiler trace (overlap, bucket sizes).

10:30 MEASURE — Scaling table: strategy, GPUs, tokens/s, efficiency, peak memory per GPU. Plot tokens/s vs N for 1, 2, 4. Profiler screenshots showing exposed communication for TP over PCIe vs overlapped all-reduce for DDP.

12:00 TAKEAWAY — Measure the interconnect first; it predicts which strategy scales. Interview line: for a model that fits on one GPU, DDP or FSDP beats tensor parallelism, and TP only pays off with NVLink and models too large for data parallelism alone.
12:45 NEXT — Next: MFU, checkpoints and failures at scale.

gotchas: Measuring tokens/s including the first steps where torch.compile and NCCL warm up; comparing strategies at different global batch sizes so efficiency numbers are meaningless; NCCL_P2P_DISABLE or a cloud topology without peer-to-peer silently routes through host memory, check NCCL_DEBUG=INFO output.
interview_q: You have 4 GPUs connected by PCIe and a 1B model that fits on one GPU. Which parallelism do you use? Data parallelism, DDP or FSDP, because it communicates once per step and overlaps with backward; tensor parallelism all-reduces activations every layer and over PCIe that exposed communication usually makes it slower than one GPU's scaling would suggest.
explainer: Here is our four GPU pod. Before training anything, we ask the hardware how its GPUs are connected.
The topology map says whether they talk over NVLink or PCIe. That one fact predicts most of what follows.
nccl tests measures the real bus bandwidth. That number is the ceiling for every strategy.
Now training. DDP on four GPUs. All reduce hides behind backward, and throughput nearly quadruples.
FSDP adds an extra all gather. Slightly slower than DDP, but memory per GPU drops.
Tensor parallel all reduces activations every layer. Over PCIe, those transfers sit right on the critical path.
In the profiler trace you can see it. Long communication bars with idle compute beside them.
Four strategies, one loss curve. They all learn the same thing. They just pay different communication taxes.

hook: Llama 3's training run hit 419 unexpected interruptions in 54 days. At scale, checkpointing and MFU matter as much as the model.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Llama 3's training run hit 419 unexpected interruptions in 54 days. At scale, checkpointing and MFU matter as much as the model.

0:15 QUESTION — MFU is the number every pretraining team reports: what fraction of the hardware's peak FLOPs went into the model. PaLM reported 46 percent. Failures are the other half of large-scale life. We compute MFU for our RunPod run, add async distributed checkpoints, and kill a rank on purpose.

1:00 INTUITION — MFU is a fuel efficiency gauge: useful work divided by what the engine could do flat out. Recomputation, communication stalls and small kernels all burn fuel without moving the car. Checkpoints are save points in a long game; the trick is saving without pausing play. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:00 MATH — Training FLOPs per token approx 6 N (2 forward, 4 backward) plus attention 12 L h s (PaLM appendix formula, with h = d_model, s = sequence length). MFU = tokens_per_sec * (6 N + 12 L h s) / (n_gpus * peak_flops). HFU also counts recomputed FLOPs, so HFU is at least MFU. Peak must be the dense bf16 number for the GPU (for example 989 TFLOPs for H100 SXM, 312 for A100), not the sparse one. Checkpoint cost: state bytes 16 Psi; save time = bytes / storage bandwidth; with async save, blocking time is only the device to host copy. Optimal checkpoint interval (Young's approximation): sqrt(2 * checkpoint_time * MTBF).

4:30 CODE — def mfu(tokens_per_sec, n_params, n_layers, d_model, seq_len, n_gpus, peak) and cross-check against nanoGPT's estimate_mfu, which uses the same 6N + 12 L h s form. Checkpointing with torch.distributed.checkpoint: dcp.save(state_dict, checkpoint_id=path) using get_state_dict(model, optimizer) from torch.distributed.checkpoint.state_dict, then dcp.async_save for the non-blocking version. Failure drill: launch with torchrun --nnodes=1 --nproc_per_node=4 --max-restarts=3, have rank 2 os._exit(1) at step 150, resume from the latest checkpoint, including dataloader position and RNG states.

8:30 RECEIPT — Your mfu() equals nanoGPT's estimate_mfu for the same model config and throughput (adjusted to the same peak). Plug PaLM 540B's published throughput and config into your formula and land near its reported 46.2 percent MFU. Resume correctness: loss at steps 151 to 200 after the crash-and-restart torch.testing.assert_close to an uninterrupted run (deterministic data order, same seeds). Resharding: save with 4 ranks, load with 2, and the model state_dict matches.

10:30 MEASURE — MFU for each strategy from E15, a bar chart against the published 30 to 50 percent range for large runs. Blocking time per checkpoint: dcp.save vs dcp.async_save. Timeline of the failure drill showing lost steps.

12:00 TAKEAWAY — Report MFU with 6N plus attention FLOPs over dense peak, save sharded checkpoints asynchronously, and practice restarts before you need them. Interview line: MFU counts only model FLOPs, so recomputation raises HFU but not MFU, and checkpoint frequency should balance save cost against mean time between failures.

gotchas: Using the sparse-FLOPs peak from the spec sheet halves your reported MFU, always use the dense bf16 number; resuming without the dataloader position so the model re-sees the same data; modifying parameters while dcp.async_save is still copying them, wait on the returned future before the next optimizer step.
interview_q: How do you compute MFU and why can it differ from HFU? MFU is tokens per second times model FLOPs per token, about 6N plus attention FLOPs, divided by the cluster's dense peak FLOPs; HFU also counts recomputed FLOPs from activation checkpointing, so a run with recomputation has higher HFU than MFU.
explainer: Here is a fuel gauge for training. Model FLOPs used, divided by what the GPUs could do at full tilt.
Each token costs about six FLOPs per parameter. Two forward, four backward. Plus a term for attention.
Multiply by tokens per second, then divide by the number of GPUs times their peak. That ratio is MFU.
Recomputation does real work but not new model work. It raises hardware utilization, not MFU.
Now failures. A long run is a long game, and crashes are guaranteed at scale.
Distributed checkpoints save each rank's shard in parallel. Async save copies to CPU and keeps training.
We kill rank two at step one fifty. torchrun restarts the job, and it resumes from the last save.
The loss curve after the crash lines up exactly with a run that never crashed.
